newsitem.title: DUBAI: Mid East Gulf oil producers pray for repeat of 1996.
newsitem.headline: Mid East Gulf oil producers pray for repeat of 1996.

text.p: The oil powerhouses of the Middle East Gulf will be crossing their fingers next year in the hope that the petrodollars keep piling up after a bonus windfall in 1996.
With oil prices bubbling at their highest level since the 1990-1991 Gulf War, state coffers from Riyadh to Tehran are brimming and there are no clear signs of a serious price fall.

"It has been spectacular on the revenue side. They (Gulf producers) would be more than pleased if next year proves to be anywhere near as good as this year," said one Western executive based in the Gulf.
Analysts project that Saudi Arabia has earned up to $10 billion above it's revenue forecast in this year's budget and is on course to reverse 14 years of heavy deficit financing.

The debt-ridden producers have also seen this month the limited return of Iraqi crude to the market for the first time in six years -- without major ripples in international prices, defying earlier predictions of a major price slump.
Confident that after years of sluggish oil prices that failed to keep up with inflation, producers in the region are hoping that higher prices will not be a passing mirage.
Gulf sources expect prices to continue in a range of $20-25 for North Sea Brent in 1997, compared to prices of between $15-20 that have been dominant for the last 10 years.
A barrel of Saudi Arabia's six million barrels per day (bpd) of crude exports on Monday was at $22.00-$22.50, compared to an estimated budget price of $14 and $16.50 exactly a year ago.
But some dark clouds are emerging on the horizon for Gulf producers who between them own nearly 70 percent of global oil reserves and provide 30 percent of world supplies.

"Iraq's return will weigh increasingly on the supply-demand balance as 1997 progresses. Barring Middle East worries, oil prices should return gradually to more normal (lower) levels in the face of rising supply," said energy analyst Mehdi Varzi at finance house Kleinwort Benson.

The most pressing concern next year may turn out to be increasing supplies from exporters outside the control of the Organisation of the Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) and how the market absorbs Iraqi oil once winter heating fuel demand eases.
Lack of internal OPEC production discipline -- particularly reported quota busting by Venezuela and Nigeria -- may also harm Gulf states' hopes for tight supplies in 1997.
Supplies from the British and Norwegian North Sea are set to lead a four percent rise in non-OPEC supplies next year, so grabbing the lion's share of an increase in global oil demand.
Concern in the region centres on the political stability of Saudi Arabia, after two bomb attacks in just over a year, and the health of King Fahd, analysts say.
United States' sanctions policy towards Iran and Iraq and also lingering intra-Gulf bickering over frontiers and renewed allegations of interference in domestic affairs will also be watched closely.

Oil markets are acutely sensitive to any sign of instability or change in Saudi Arabia -- the world's largest oil producer and exporter -- whether it be over the succession or domestic challenges to the regime or Western interests in the kingdom.

Markets, crude clients and firms aiming for business in the multi-billion dollar energy equipment market will also be focused on Washington's application of sanctions on firms that invest $40 million or more a year in Iran's oil or gas sectors.
Tehran, for its part, is set to announce its preferred foreign partners in a host of projects for the country and will begin work on a pipeline project to ship gas to Turkey.
